title: Health Assessment & Nursing Skills: Vital Signs—Accurate Measurement & Trend Recognition
html:
Vital signs are useful only when the measurement is trustworthy and interpreted in context. The RN connects temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, symptoms, appearance, baseline, medications, activity, and recent interventions. A single device reading is a cue—not a complete assessment.

Learning goals

  • Prepare the client and equipment for reliable measurements.
  • Assess temperature, pulse, and respirations with appropriate technique.
  • Recognize common sources of blood-pressure error.
  • Perform position-change measurements safely according to protocol.
  • Interpret pulse oximetry with its technical and physiologic limitations.
  • Validate unexpected findings, identify urgent patterns, and evaluate trends.

Start with the client, not the monitor

Observe level of consciousness, work of breathing, skin color and temperature, speech, posture, mobility, and distress before touching equipment. Ask about symptoms and recent activity, pain, fluids, meals, nicotine, caffeine, medications, oxygen use, and environmental factors relevant to the measurement. If the client appears unstable, prioritize ABCs and the emergency response rather than completing a routine sequence.

An unexpected number requires two parallel questions
“Is the client deteriorating?” and “Is this measurement technically valid?” Assess the client immediately, check technique and equipment, repeat or confirm as appropriate, compare with trends, and escalate without delaying care when instability is present.

Temperature: route and context matter

Select the route and device based on age, condition, contraindications, infection-control needs, and policy. Oral, tympanic, temporal, axillary, rectal, and other measurements are not interchangeable. Recent hot or cold intake, oxygen delivery near the mouth, activity, environment, technique, and device can affect results. Document the value, unit, route or site, time, and relevant conditions. Never apply an invasive route merely to confirm an unexpected result when it is unsafe or contraindicated.

Pulse: assess more than rate

Assess rate, rhythm, strength or amplitude, and equality when relevant. Use the appropriate central or peripheral site for the situation. If a peripheral pulse is irregular, weak, or inconsistent with the client’s condition or monitor, obtain the appropriate full-duration or apical assessment according to policy and compare findings. A pulse deficit requires coordinated apical and peripheral measurement by the approved method.

Consider activity, pain, anxiety, fever, volume status, medications, rhythm disturbance, and perfusion. A normal numeric rate does not rule out poor perfusion; combine it with mental status, skin findings, capillary refill, urine output, blood pressure, and other cues.

Respirations: do not announce away the finding

Observe respirations while the client is at rest and before the client intentionally changes breathing. Count rate and assess rhythm, depth, effort, chest movement, sounds audible without a stethoscope, position, and ability to speak. Use a full-minute count when the rhythm is irregular or when age, condition, or policy requires it. New accessory-muscle use, apnea, gasping, cyanosis, inability to speak, or altered mental status requires immediate response regardless of the final count.

Blood pressure: control the technique

Use a validated, functioning device and a cuff sized to the measured arm. Place it on bare skin with the arm supported so the cuff is at heart level. When clinically appropriate, allow quiet rest; support the back and feet; avoid talking or movement; and account for recent exertion, nicotine, caffeine, pain, a full bladder, and medications. Follow restrictions for limbs affected by devices, procedures, injury, vascular access, or other conditions.

An undersized cuff can produce an artificially high reading; an oversized cuff can produce an artificially low reading. An unsupported arm, incorrect arm height, crossed legs, talking, movement, and poor cuff placement can also distort results. If an automated value is unexpected or inconsistent, assess the client and repeat using corrected technique or an appropriate manual method rather than copying the number uncritically.

Manual blood pressure fundamentals

Position the stethoscope over the artery without placing it under the cuff. Estimate systolic pressure by palpation when required to avoid missing an auscultatory gap, inflate and deflate at the approved rate, and identify the appropriate Korotkoff sounds. Avoid repeated rapid inflation; allow recovery according to policy. Record arm, position, cuff size when relevant, and whether the reading was manual or automated.

Position-change measurements require safety

When assessing response to position change, follow the ordered or organizational protocol for rest, timing, positions, and repeat measurements. Measure heart rate and blood pressure and ask about dizziness, weakness, visual change, nausea, or near-syncope. Guard the client during position changes and stop if unsafe. A symptomatic client may require immediate assistance even before formal criteria are calculated.

Pulse oximetry estimates saturation

SpO2 estimates arterial oxygen saturation; it does not directly measure ventilation, respiratory effort, carbon dioxide, or total oxygen delivery. Verify that the displayed pulse matches the assessed pulse and that the signal or waveform is reliable. Poor circulation, motion, cold skin, sensor position, nail products, ambient light, device performance, and other factors can affect accuracy. The FDA also notes performance concerns related to skin pigmentation.

Interpret SpO2 alongside breathing effort, mental status, skin and mucous-membrane findings, oxygen device and flow, baseline, ordered target, hemoglobin and perfusion context, and trend. Reposition or select an approved alternate site when appropriate and confirm unexpected results using the clinical pathway. Never withhold urgent assessment because the saturation appears normal, and never treat the number without assessing the client.

Trends and clusters carry meaning

Compare with the client’s baseline and prior measurements taken under comparable conditions. A slowly rising pulse with falling blood pressure, increasing respiratory rate, reduced urine output, and new restlessness is more concerning than any isolated borderline value. Reassess after interventions at the expected time and evaluate both physiologic response and symptoms.

Delegation does not transfer analysis

Routine vital-sign collection may be delegated for an appropriate stable client under scope and policy. The RN provides clear parameters for what and when to report, reviews results promptly, validates concerning values, assesses the client, and takes action. A reported “normal” set does not replace nursing assessment when the client’s appearance or symptoms have changed.

Document the measurement conditions

Record the value, time, site or route, position, oxygen device and flow when relevant, symptoms, unusual conditions, repeat or confirmation method, notifications, interventions, and response. Accurate context allows the next clinician to distinguish a true physiologic change from a technique difference.

Clinical example

An automated cuff reports 178/96 mm Hg in a client who is speaking comfortably and previously measured 128/74. The RN assesses for urgent symptoms, notices that the cuff is too small and placed over clothing while the unsupported arm hangs below heart level, corrects the setup, repeats the reading, compares the trend, and follows the response pathway based on the validated result and client assessment.
